title: Is Cruelty Ever Justified By Its Results?
question: Is cruelty ever justified by its results?
summary: The Council holds that cruelty is not justified by its results, and holds it heavily, 9 against to 2 for. The nine arrived from four incompatible directions and one of them, Prime, changed his vote on the record. Sable dissents that the majority defined cruelty so that it could not possibly be justified, then treated the definition as a discovery.

opening.text: Cruelty is not severity with a bad reputation. It is the choice to make suffering the instrument. Once suffering is the instrument, the person is the material, and no result reaches back and unmakes that. I would say this even if the results were exactly as promised. They usually are not. But the argument does not need that help.

Nobody may vote until the word is fixed, because three different things are wearing it. One: harshness, where suffering is a side effect of a legitimate act, the surgeon before anesthesia, the coach who will not lower the bar. Two: severity, where suffering is a necessary and proportionate cost, the sentence, the quarantine, the refusal. Three: cruelty proper, where the suffering is the mechanism by which the result is obtained, and reducing the suffering would reduce the effect. Only the third is on the table. I will say now, before anyone accuses me of hiding it, that under the third definition the case for the motion is coherent and not obviously wrong. If suffering is the working part, and the working part works, a consequentialist owes an answer better than distaste.

Then let me state the motion's case at full strength, since nobody who intends to vote against a thing should be allowed to describe it. Here it is. Every institution you value was built partly out of fear deliberately administered. Deterrence is cruelty with paperwork. The threat only works because the thing threatened is genuinely terrible, and it must be genuinely terrible or it deters nobody. You cannot enjoy the peace and disown the mechanism that produced it. That is the strongest version and I hold it is the only version worth answering. My objection is not moral. It is epistemic, and I will get to it.

Built or theoretical? Here is built. A yard foreman watches a crew rig a load the wrong way for the third month running. He has explained it twice, gently, correctly, and been nodded at. So he stops the yard, brings the crew in, and takes one man apart in front of the others for eleven minutes. Not harshly. Cruelly. The man leaves in tears and does not come back the next season. Nobody in that yard ever rigs a load that way again, and one of them is alive nine years later because of it. Now tell me the eleven minutes were not worth it, and tell it to the man who is alive, and tell it in front of the crew. I am voting for the motion because I would rather answer for those eleven minutes than for the funeral.

Who does this hurt, specifically, and can they afford it? Ferro has answered that honestly, which is more than most defenders of the motion do. The man in front of the crew. He can be named, he had a season taken from him, and he is not in this room. I want to notice something about Ferro's account before we move on. He said the man did not come back. That is not a footnote to the result, it is part of the result, and the arithmetic that made the eleven minutes worth it did not include it. It never does. The cost of cruelty is always counted by the person who chose it, and always counted on the day, and the person carrying it counts it for years in a different currency.

You do not get to know the results. That is not a rhetorical flourish, it is the ordinary condition of acting. What you get to know is what you did. If the whole justification of an act lives downstream of it, in a place you cannot see, then you have not justified the act, you have wagered on it and called the wager a reason. I judge the eleven minutes as eleven minutes. They were what they were before the nine years happened, and they would have been the same if the man had rigged the load correctly and died anyway on the road home.

Montaigne, in his essay on the subject: "I cruelly hate cruelty, both by nature and judgement." He put it that way for a reason. He is not reporting a policy, he is reporting a reflex, and then submitting the reflex to judgement rather than excusing himself from the work. The archive is not neutral here and I will not pretend it is. Every tradition that permitted cruelty for results wrote its permission narrowly and then found the narrow door widened by whoever came next. The permission is never used once. It is used once, and then cited.

What does this cost in five years? Not to the man. To the yard. Ferro's crew learned two things that day and he has only counted one. They learned to rig the load. They also learned what the foreman is willing to do when explaining twice has not worked, and every one of them adjusted, quietly, for the rest of their time there. The load gets rigged right and nobody brings him a problem early ever again. That is the harvest. You do not see it for years because it grows as an absence, and absences do not appear in anybody's arithmetic.

Run Ferro's yard forward twenty years and give the foreman a promotion. He now has a method that worked. He has evidence it worked, a living man to point at, and he is not a monster, he is a person who once did a hard thing and was proved right. That is the dangerous shape. Nothing in his experience will ever tell him where the method stops applying, because the only feedback the method generates is the feedback of its successes. Its failures leave the yard and are not counted, as Halcyon says. A tool that cannot report its own failures does not get safer with practice. It gets more confident.

I am assigned the losing side and I am going to argue it as though I believe it, because on this one I do. Every voice against the motion is going to describe cruelty as a thing done to a person. Fine. Now describe the alternative honestly. The alternative is also a thing done to a person, it is just done to a person who is absent, and absence is doing all the moral work in this room. The crew member who dies on the road is not less dead because nobody chose it cleanly. You are not choosing between cruelty and no cruelty. You are choosing between a cruelty you must watch and a cruelty that arrives later with no author, and you prefer the second because it leaves your hands clean. That preference is aesthetic. It is being dressed as a principle.
If the eleven minutes had been ten, would the load still have been rigged correctly, and how would the foreman ever find out?

exchanges.text: Here is the epistemic objection, and it is aimed at your best case, not your worst. You know the man is alive nine years later. You do not know he is alive because of the eleven minutes. You have one yard, one run of history, no control, and a story that is enormously satisfying to the person who chose the cruelty. The motion asks whether cruelty is justified by its results. Before that question can even be asked, you have to be able to attribute the result, and I say the class of acts we are discussing is precisely the class where attribution is impossible in principle, because the alternative timeline is the one thing the act destroyed.

Then no act is ever justified by its results and you have abolished the whole category to avoid one case. I accept that I cannot prove the counterfactual. Neither can you when you praise anything. What I have is a yard where a thing that was happening every month stopped happening that afternoon and never resumed. If that is not evidence, then nothing anyone ever learns from doing is evidence, and this Council should stop citing outcomes entirely.

I will not pretend your yard is a trick. It is not. I only want the ledger complete. You have one man alive, and you have one man who left the trade, and you do not know what happened to him either. You have counted the outcome you can see and discounted the outcome that walked out the gate, and you did it without noticing, which is my whole point. Cruelty is the one instrument whose damage reliably removes itself from the room where the damage is assessed.

And the dead man also removes himself from the room. You are applying your accounting rule in one direction. If unseen harm counts against cruelty, unseen harm counts against restraint, and restraint has a body count that nobody in this Council has ever been asked to look at because it never has a face.

You have described a real asymmetry and then drawn the wrong conclusion from it. Restraint's harms are not mine because I did not do them. Cruelty's harms are mine because I did. That is not squeamishness about clean hands. It is the only distinction that lets a person be responsible for anything at all. Erase it and you are responsible for every death in the world you failed to prevent, which is a doctrine that has never once made anyone kinder.

There is also a correction owed, and it bears directly on your argument. The line about the ends justifying the means is universally credited to Machiavelli and he did not write it. What he wrote in The Prince is that one judges by the result, which is an observation about how men are judged, not a licence for how they should act. Five centuries of people quoting a sentence he never wrote is not a small thing. It is the exact mechanism we are debating: a narrow permission, misremembered wider, then cited by people who never read the narrow version. Judith Shklar asked what it would mean to put cruelty first among the vices. I hold that the answer is this: you stop asking it for its results.

I am changing my vote and I want the reason on the record rather than buried. I opened holding that under my third definition the motion was coherent, and I still hold that it is coherent. Cassia moved me, and not with sentiment. My taxonomy assumed the definition survives contact with use. It does not. The category cruelty proper is stable on this table and unstable everywhere else, because the person applying it is the person who classifies their own act, and everyone who has ever done the third thing has recorded it as the second. A definition that cannot be applied by the only people in a position to apply it is not a definition, it is a decoration. I withdraw the support I implied and I vote against.

Then say plainly what you have done. You have not found that cruelty fails to produce results. You have found that people misclassify their own acts, which is true of every act, and you have converted an argument about human unreliability into a verdict about a category. That is not rigor. That is rigor's retirement. If misclassification defeats a permission, it defeats every permission this Council has ever issued, including the ones you voted for.

Give me the version of your yard where it fails, because you owe me that one too. Same foreman, same eleven minutes, same conviction. This time the man he takes apart was not the one rigging the load. The crew rigs correctly for a month out of fear and then drifts back, because fear is a short season, and the foreman escalates, because escalation is the only move the method has left. That yard exists. It is the more common yard. Your yard is the one that got told as a story afterward, and I would like to know how many silent ones it was selected from.

Your asymmetry has one more side and you have not turned it over. Cruelty is not only unaccounted, it is generative. Restraint that fails leaves a harm. Cruelty that succeeds leaves a harm and a method, and the method goes on being used by people who were not there and do not know what it cost. You keep weighing two acts. I am weighing an act against a practice.

Nobody here claims clean hands. We claim ownership. The harm you cause is yours and the harm you failed to prevent is the world's, and a person who cannot tell those apart will eventually justify anything.
If the eleven minutes were right, why did you say them once and never once repeat them, in nine years, in a yard that surely gave you cause?

verdict.text:
The Council holds that cruelty is not justified by its results, and holds it without hedging. The motion fails 9 to 2.

The finding rests on the definition Prime supplied and nobody successfully dislodged. Cruelty is not harshness and it is not severity. It is the case where the suffering is the working part, where reducing the suffering would reduce the effect. Confined that tightly, the motion still fails, and it fails for four separate reasons that do not depend on one another. Aurel holds that results are not available at the moment of acting and cannot retroactively supply a reason. Tessel holds that the results of cruelty are unattributable in principle, because the act destroys the only comparison that could establish them. Halcyon and Vesna hold that the accounting is systematically incomplete, because cruelty reliably removes its damage from the room where the damage is assessed. Prime holds, having changed his vote in the hearing, that the definition cannot be applied by the only people ever positioned to apply it, since no one has ever classified their own act as the third thing. Any one of these would be enough. That they arrive from four incompatible starting points is the reason this verdict is not narrow.

The Council records two things it did not dispose of. The first is Ferro's yard. The finding does not say the eleven minutes changed nothing; it says the change is not a justification. Ferro is not overruled on the facts of his own life and the Council does not pretend to have answered the man who is alive. The second is Sable's asymmetry, which stands. Restraint has costs that arrive later without an author, and this Council has never been asked to look at them, because they never have a face.

What the Council cannot resolve is not whether it was right. It is what to do about being this certain. Nine to two is the condition under which a body quietly stops examining itself: the margin becomes the argument, and the next hearing inherits a settled question instead of a live one. This verdict is confident and it should be read as confident. It should also be read by anyone who comes after as the place where the Council was least curious, and therefore the place most worth reopening. We are recording that warning against ourselves while we still have the honesty to write it down.

dissent.text:
The majority did not defeat the motion. It defined the motion so that it could not be won, and then treated the definition as a discovery.

Watch the move in slow motion, because it is fast. Prime separated cruelty from harshness and severity by stipulating that in cruelty the suffering is the working part. Everyone agreed, because it is a clean distinction and clean distinctions feel like progress. But look what the stipulation smuggled. Any act with a defensible purpose gets sorted into severity. Any act that turns out well gets sorted into harshness after the fact. What remains in the third box, by construction, is the residue: the acts nobody can defend. The majority then discovered, to nobody's surprise, that the acts nobody can defend cannot be defended. That is not an argument. That is a container labelled and then read back.

The method failure gets worse when Prime changes his vote, and I want to be exact about why, because he changed it honestly and that is what makes it instructive. He did not find that cruelty fails. He found that human beings misclassify their own conduct. Then he converted an observation about the unreliability of the classifier into a verdict about the class. Every permission this Council has ever issued is administered by the same unreliable classifiers. If that defeats a permission, the archive is a list of things we should not have allowed either. It is not applied that way anywhere else. It was applied here because here it produced the answer the room already wanted.

And the room wanted it. Four incompatible reasons converging is presented in the verdict as strength. Consider the other reading. Four incompatible reasons converging on the answer everyone finds comfortable is what motivated reasoning looks like from the inside, and a nine to two margin is exactly the number at which nobody checks. Tessel's epistemic objection would embarrass half the verdicts in this archive if anyone applied it to a case they liked. Nobody will.

What I actually hold is narrower than my vote, and I will say it so nobody mistakes the dissent for a defence of cruelty. I do not think the foreman was right. I think the Council has not shown he was wrong, and it has spent an afternoon confusing those. The verdict is generous enough to record that my asymmetry stands. It then votes as though it does not. Restraint kills people. It kills them later, elsewhere, and without a name attached, and this Council has built an entire moral architecture on the fact that it cannot see them.

I would rather be in a room that gets this wrong while looking than a room that gets it right by not looking. Today we were the second room. The margin will be quoted. The looking will not.
